title: Helminth Specimens: Pinworm Tape, Taenia Eggs, Schistosome Spines and Microfilariae Timing
summary: Learn why pinworm needs perianal tape rather than stool, why Taenia eggs are reported only as Taenia species, how the spine separates Schistosoma eggs and where each is found, and when to draw blood for nocturnal and diurnal microfilariae.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 65 Hits 7, 10, 11 and 12 and Traps 4 and 5. Pinworm points from CDC DPDx (Enterobiasis; read via a page-fetch tool) and Wendt 2019; Taenia from CDC DPDx (Taeniasis; read via a page-fetch tool) and Ng-Nguyen 2017; schistosome eggs from CDC DPDx (Schistosomiasis; read via a page-fetch tool), Gray 2011 and Ponzo 2024; microfilariae timing from CDC DPDx (Lymphatic filariasis, Loiasis; read via a page-fetch tool) and Pietrzak 2024. CDC pages could not be downloaded directly (HTTP 403 to the command-line client) and were read only through a page-fetch tool. Hit 10 and the Number Vault give Taenia eggs as 31–43 μm; CDC gives 30–35 μm (register flag rv-taenia-egg-size-range). Hit 11 gives the S. haematobium urine window as 10 am–2 pm; Gray 2011 and Ponzo 2024 agree, but CDC DPDx gives noon–3 pm (register flag rv-haematobium-urine-window). The “5–10% of infections show up in stool” figure (Hit 7, Trap 5) was not found in the sources read; sources say only that stool detects eggs less often (register flag rv-pinworm-stool-yield-figure). A 2022 single-centre study (Machrumnizar, Iran J Parasitol) reported Ziehl–Neelsen staining as an experimental way to separate T. saginata and T. solium eggs; it is not taught. Schistosome egg sizes are taught from CDC, which differ slightly from the Number Vault. The Loa loa contrast in Hit 12 is supported by CDC and Pietrzak 2024. Not taught: S. intercalatum and S. mekongi details, cysticercosis serology, treatment.

objectives: Choose the correct specimen and collection time for suspected Enterobius vermicularis.
Explain why Taenia eggs are reported as Taenia species and name the methods that identify the species.
Identify S. mansoni, S. haematobium and S. japonicum eggs by spine and specimen type.
State the blood collection windows for nocturnal (W. bancrofti, Brugia) and diurnal (Loa loa) microfilariae.

scenes.title: Three requests, wrong specimens
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three requests reach the parasitology bench. (1) A 6-year-old with night-time perianal itching: the order is “stool O&P”. (2) A stool shows round, radially striated eggs with six hooks inside; the clinician asks “T. solium or T. saginata?”. (3) A traveller from a filariasis-endemic area with leg swelling: blood drawn at 9 am for microfilariae. Question token: “Right specimen, right time, right report?”

cues.text: Three requests reach the parasitology bench. A six-year-old with itching around the anus at night, and the order is a stool exam.
A stool with round, striated tapeworm eggs, and the clinician wants to know: pork tapeworm or beef tapeworm? And a traveller with a swollen leg, blood drawn at nine in the morning for microfilariae.
Is each one the right specimen, collected at the right time, with the right report?

props.label: Right specimen, right time, right report?

scenes.title: Where each parasite leaves its evidence
scenes.altText: Four cards. Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis): eggs are deposited on the perianal skin, outside the intestine, so perianal tape is the method of choice; eggs are found in stool less frequently; eggs 50–60 × 20–30 μm, elongate-oval, flattened on one side. Taenia: eggs or proglottids in stool; eggs about 30–35 μm, round, radially striated, with a six-hooked oncosphere; all Taenia species produce morphologically identical eggs. Schistosoma: S. mansoni and S. japonicum eggs in stool; S. haematobium eggs in urine. Filariae: W. bancrofti and Brugia microfilariae circulate in blood, sheathed, with periodicity.

cues.text: Each parasite leaves its evidence in a different place. The pinworm’s eggs are deposited outside the gut, on the skin around the anus, so tape from that skin is the method of choice; eggs turn up in stool less often. The egg is oval and flattened on one side.

Taenia tapeworms shed eggs and segments, called proglottids, into the stool. The egg is round, about thirty to thirty-five micrometres, radially striated, with six hooks inside. Every Taenia species makes the same egg.
Schistosomes split by organ: Schistosoma mansoni and japonicum eggs come out in stool, but Schistosoma haematobium eggs come out in urine.
Filarial worms such as Wuchereria bancrofti release sheathed microfilariae into the blood, but not at every hour of the day.

scenes.title: The clock decides the yield
scenes.altText: Timing cards. Pinworm: press clear cellulose tape on perianal skin in the morning, before defecation and washing; repeat on three different days (one test about 50% sensitive, three about 90%). W. bancrofti and Brugia: nocturnal periodicity, blood best drawn 10 pm–2 am. Loa loa: diurnal periodicity, blood best drawn 10 am–2 pm. Circulating filarial antigen (W. bancrofti) can be detected in blood taken at any time of day. S. haematobium: urine collected around midday — 10 am–2 pm in a BMJ review and a 2024 review (terminal urine), noon–3 pm in CDC DPDx.

cues.text: For pinworm, press clear tape on the perianal skin in the morning, before the first bowel movement and before washing. One tape catches about half of infections; tapes on three different days catch about ninety percent.

Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia microfilariae are nocturnal: draw blood between ten at night and two in the morning. Loa loa is the opposite, diurnal: draw blood between ten in the morning and two in the afternoon.
For Wuchereria bancrofti, tests for circulating filarial antigen escape the clock: the antigen can be detected in blood taken at any time of day.
Schistosoma haematobium egg output in urine peaks around midday. Reviews give ten in the morning to two in the afternoon, while CDC gives noon to three, so follow your laboratory’s procedure.

scenes.title: Reading spines and naming tapeworms
scenes.altText: Schistosome egg cards (CDC DPDx sizes): S. mansoni 114–180 × 45–70 μm, prominent lateral spine near the posterior end (stool); S. haematobium 110–170 × 40–70 μm, conspicuous terminal spine (urine); S. japonicum 70–100 × 55–64 μm, smaller and rounder with a small, inconspicuous spine (stool). Taenia card: eggs cannot name the species; report “Taenia species”; species are separated by gravid proglottids (primary lateral uterine branches: T. saginata 12–30, T. solium 7–13), by the scolex (T. solium has hooks, T. saginata none) or by molecular tests on stool (multiplex real-time PCR). Hook answers: (1) perianal tape, morning, three days; (2) report “Taenia species”, send proglottids or a molecular test; (3) redraw blood 10 pm–2 am or test filarial antigen.

cues.text: Schistosome eggs are read by their spine. Schistosoma mansoni: a large egg with a prominent lateral spine. Schistosoma haematobium: a large egg with a terminal spine. Schistosoma japonicum: smaller and rounder, with a small, inconspicuous spine.

Taenia eggs cannot name the species, so the report says Taenia species. To separate them, count the main side branches of the uterus in a gravid proglottid: about twelve to thirty for the beef tapeworm, seven to thirteen for the pork tapeworm. Between these two, a scolex with hooks means Taenia solium, and molecular tests on stool can also tell them apart.

Back to the hook. The child needs perianal tape in the morning, on three different days, not a stool exam. The tapeworm eggs are reported as Taenia species, with proglottids or a molecular test to name the species.
The traveller’s morning blood is the wrong time for Wuchereria bancrofti: redraw between ten at night and two in the morning, or test for filarial antigen.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Order stool O&P for suspected pinworm” (✓ perianal tape in the morning; eggs are deposited outside the gut and appear in stool less often); “Name T. solium or T. saginata from the egg” (✓ all Taenia eggs look the same: report Taenia species); “Draw blood for W. bancrofti at any convenient time” (✓ nocturnal: 10 pm–2 am; Loa loa is the daytime one).

cues.text: Trap one: send stool for suspected pinworm. No: the eggs are deposited on the perianal skin, so use tape in the morning.
Trap two: name the Taenia species from the egg. No: all Taenia eggs look the same. Report Taenia species.
Trap three: draw blood for Wuchereria bancrofti whenever convenient. No: it is nocturnal, ten at night to two in the morning. Loa loa is the daytime filaria.

props.title: ✗ “Bancrofti blood any time.”
lines: ✓ 10 pm–2 am; Loa loa by day

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Pinworm = perianal tape at dawn · Taenia eggs = report Taenia species”, “Schistosoma spine names the species · haematobium in midday urine · bancrofti blood 10 pm–2 am”.

cues.text: Match the specimen and the clock to the parasite: perianal tape in the morning for pinworm, Taenia eggs reported only as Taenia species, the egg spine and midday urine for Schistosoma, and night blood for Wuchereria bancrofti.

props.label: Pinworm = tape at dawn · Taenia egg = “Taenia species”
Spine names Schistosoma · midday urine · bancrofti 10 pm–2 am

explanation.what: Plain language: worms leave their eggs or larvae in different places at different times, so the lab must sample the right place at the right hour, and some eggs cannot tell you the exact species. Scientific terms: Enterobius vermicularis, cellulose tape (Scotch) test, Taenia solium, T. saginata, proglottid, uterine branches, scolex, oncosphere, Schistosoma mansoni, S. haematobium, S. japonicum, lateral and terminal spine, microfilariae, nocturnal and diurnal periodicity, circulating filarial antigen.
explanation.why: A wrong specimen or wrong time gives a false negative: pinworm eggs are deposited outside the intestine, S. haematobium eggs leave in urine, and blood microfilariae peak at set hours. Over-calling a Taenia species from an egg is wrong because all Taenia eggs look the same, and the species matters because ingested T. solium eggs can cause cysticercosis.
explanation.measure: Pinworm: perianal tape in the morning before defecation and washing, on 3 different days (~50% single, ~90% three); egg 50–60 × 20–30 μm, flattened on one side. Taenia: egg ~30–35 μm, radially striated, six hooks; report Taenia species; proglottid uterine branches T. saginata 12–30, T. solium 7–13; hooked scolex = T. solium; multiplex real-time PCR differentiates species in stool. Schistosoma (CDC): mansoni 114–180 × 45–70 μm lateral spine (stool); haematobium 110–170 × 40–70 μm terminal spine (urine, around midday: 10 am–2 pm in reviews, noon–3 pm in CDC); japonicum 70–100 × 55–64 μm, small inconspicuous spine (stool). Microfilariae: W. bancrofti and Brugia 10 pm–2 am; Loa loa 10 am–2 pm; W. bancrofti circulating antigen detectable at any time of day.
explanation.differs: Tape (pinworm) vs stool O&P (Taenia, S. mansoni, S. japonicum); egg (genus only) vs proglottid, scolex or PCR (species) for Taenia; lateral vs terminal vs small spine for schistosomes; nocturnal (W. bancrofti, Brugia) vs diurnal (Loa loa) microfilariae; microscopy (time-dependent) vs antigen tests (any time).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: best specimen for suspected pinworm after negative stools, the correct report for a Taenia egg, naming a schistosome from its spine or specimen, and the right blood draw time for W. bancrofti vs Loa loa.

mnemonic.text: Tape at DAWN for the pinworm; the Taenia egg is NAMELESS; the SPINE points the way (side = mansoni, tip = haematobium in urine at lunchtime); Bancrofti is a NIGHT OWL, Loa loa a LUNCH guest.

mnemonic.limitation: Sources give different midday urine windows (10 am–2 pm vs noon–3 pm); some filarial strains are sub-periodic and antigen tests ignore the clock; proglottids, scolex or molecular tests can name the Taenia species.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has intense perianal itching at night. Three stool O&P examinations were negative. What is the best next specimen?

options.text: Clear cellulose tape pressed on the perianal skin in the morning, before washing or defecation
options.rationale: Correct. Enterobius eggs are deposited on the perianal skin, so perianal tape is the method of choice; repeating it on three different days raises sensitivity to about 90%.
Incorrect. Pinworm eggs are deposited outside the intestine and are found in stool less often, so perianal tape, not more stools, is the method of choice.

options.text: Tape collected in the evening after a bath
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tape should be collected in the morning, before defecation and before washing.

options.text: A blood smear drawn at night for microfilariae
options.rationale: Incorrect. Night blood is for nocturnal microfilariae such as W. bancrofti, not pinworm.

questions.stem: A stool concentrate shows round, radially striated eggs about 30–35 μm with a six-hooked oncosphere. The patient eats both pork and beef. How should the laboratory report the finding?

options.text: “Taenia species eggs”; species needs a proglottid, scolex or molecular test
options.rationale: Correct. All Taenia species produce morphologically identical eggs; proglottid uterine branches, a hooked scolex or a molecular test separate T. solium from T. saginata.

options.text: “Taenia solium eggs”, because the eggs are striated
options.rationale: Incorrect. Radial striation is shared by all Taenia eggs and does not identify T. solium.

options.text: “Taenia saginata eggs”, because beef tapeworm is more common
options.rationale: Incorrect. Diet and frequency cannot identify the species; the egg alone gives only the genus.

options.text: “Taenia species eggs”; the species can never be determined
options.rationale: Incorrect. The egg gives only the genus, but gravid proglottids, the scolex or a molecular test on stool can identify the species.

questions.stem: Lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti is suspected in a traveller. When should blood be drawn to look for microfilariae on a smear?

options.rationale: Correct. W. bancrofti microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity, so night blood (10 pm–2 am) gives the best yield.
Incorrect. Midday is the window for the diurnal Loa loa, not W. bancrofti.
Incorrect. The draw time is set by the nocturnal periodicity of W. bancrofti, so blood is best taken at night, not in the morning.

options.text: Timing does not matter for a blood smear
options.rationale: Incorrect. Timing matters for microfilariae on smears; circulating filarial antigen tests, by contrast, can use blood taken at any time of day.

references.citation: Wendt S, Trawinski H, Schubert S, Rodloff AC, Mössner J, Lübbert C. The Diagnosis and Treatment of Pinworm Infection. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2019;116(13):213-219. doi:10.3238/arztebl.2019.0213

Tape test in the morning before first bowel movement and washing; repeat on three different days; sensitivity about 50% for one test and about 90% for three; stool microscopy not helpful because eggs are deposited outside the intestine.

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. DPDx – Laboratory Identification of Parasites of Public Health Concern: Taeniasis.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (direct download blocked, HTTP 403). Eggs 30–35 μm, radially striated, six-hooked oncosphere; all Taenia eggs morphologically identical; eggs or proglottids in feces diagnostic; stool microscopy cannot be used in the first three months after infection; species separated by mature/gravid proglottids (primary lateral uterine branches T. saginata 12–30, T. solium 7–13) and scolex (T. solium rostellum with hooks); ingestion of eggs can cause cysticercosis.

references.citation: Ng-Nguyen D, Stevenson MA, Dorny P, Gabriël S, Vo TV, Nguyen VT, Phan TV, Hii SF, Traub RJ. Comparison of a new multiplex real-time PCR with the Kato Katz thick smear and copro-antigen ELISA for the detection and differentiation of Taenia spp. in human stools. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2017;11(7):e0005743. doi:10.1371/journal.pntd.0005743
references.usedFor: Microscopy cannot morphologically discriminate Taenia eggs; molecular methods (multiplex real-time PCR) detect and differentiate T. solium, T. saginata and T. asiatica in stool.

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. DPDx – Laboratory Identification of Parasites of Public Health Concern: Schistosomiasis Infection.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (direct download blocked, HTTP 403). Egg sizes and spines: S. mansoni 114–180 × 45–70 μm, prominent lateral spine; S. haematobium 110–170 × 40–70 μm, conspicuous terminal spine; S. japonicum 70–100 × 55–64 μm, smaller, less conspicuous spine; mansoni and japonicum eggs in stool, haematobium in urine; recommended urine collection noon–3 pm.

references.citation: Gray DJ, Ross AG, Li YS, McManus DP. Diagnosis and management of schistosomiasis. BMJ. 2011;342:d2651. doi:10.1136/bmj.d2651
references.usedFor: Eggs identified by size and shape with a lateral or terminal spine; S. haematobium eggs released in urine, which is ideally collected between 10 am and 2 pm to coincide with maximum egg excretion.

references.citation: Ponzo E, Midiri A, Manno A, Pastorello M, Biondo C, Mancuso G. Insights into the epidemiology, pathogenesis, and differential diagnosis of schistosomiasis. Eur J Microbiol Immunol (Bp). 2024;14(2):86-96. doi:10.1556/1886.2024.00013
references.usedFor: S. mansoni oval with prominent lateral spine; S. japonicum small and round with barely visible spine; S. haematobium prominent terminal spine, found in urine; terminal urine preferably collected 10:00 am–2:00 pm.

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. DPDx – Laboratory Identification of Parasites of Public Health Concern: Lymphatic Filariasis.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (direct download blocked, HTTP 403). W. bancrofti and Brugia microfilariae sheathed with nocturnal periodicity (sub-periodic strains exist); diagnosis best on blood collected at night; usually diagnosed from peripheral blood smears, with concentration (Knott, polycarbonate membrane filtration); filarial antigen detectable in blood collected at any time of day.

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. DPDx – Laboratory Identification of Parasites of Public Health Concern: Loiasis.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (direct download blocked, HTTP 403). Loa loa microfilariae have diurnal periodicity; diagnosis best on blood collected mid-day (10 am–2 pm).

references.citation: Pietrzak D, Łuczak JW, Wiśniewski M. Beyond Tradition: Exploring Cutting-Edge Approaches for Accurate Diagnosis of Human Filariasis. Pathogens. 2024;13(6):447. doi:10.3390/pathogens13060447
references.usedFor: W. bancrofti and Brugia nocturnal periodicity with optimal blood sampling between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.; L. loa diurnal, peak 10 a.m.–2 p.m.; antigen tests more sensitive than detecting microfilariae in night blood; no commercial B. malayi antigen test.

claims.text: Pinworm: perianal tape method of choice; morning before defecation and washing; three days (~50% vs ~90%); eggs less frequent in stool; egg size and shape.
Taenia eggs ~30–35 μm, striated, six hooks, identical across species; report Taenia species; proglottid uterine branch counts, scolex hooks and molecular tests separate species.
claims.note: Egg size range differs from the reviewer (register flag rv-taenia-egg-size-range).

claims.text: Schistosome egg spines, sizes and specimen types; S. haematobium urine around midday (10 am–2 pm in reviews, noon–3 pm in CDC).
claims.note: Urine window differs by source (register flag rv-haematobium-urine-window).

claims.text: W. bancrofti and Brugia nocturnal (10 pm–2 am); Loa loa diurnal (10 am–2 pm); microfilariae sheathed; filarial antigen detectable at any time of day.
“Only 5–10% of pinworm infections show up in stool exams” (Hit 7, Trap 5, Number Vault); Taenia egg diameter 31–43 μm; the Number Vault schistosome egg sizes.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; the lesson says stool detects pinworm eggs less often and uses CDC egg sizes (register flags rv-pinworm-stool-yield-figure, rv-taenia-egg-size-range).

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 65 Hit 10 and the Number Vault give Taenia egg diameter as 31–43 μm; CDC DPDx gives 30–35 μm. The lesson uses the CDC range (register flag rv-taenia-egg-size-range).

Ch. 65 Hit 11 gives S. haematobium urine collection as 10 am–2 pm. Gray 2011 and Ponzo 2024 agree, but CDC DPDx recommends noon–3 pm; the lesson teaches “around midday” with both windows (register flag rv-haematobium-urine-window).

Ch. 65 Hit 7, Trap 5 and the Number Vault say routine stool detects only 5–10% of pinworm infections. CDC DPDx and Wendt 2019 say eggs are found in stool less frequently or that stool microscopy is not helpful, but give no percentage; the figure is not taught (register flag rv-pinworm-stool-yield-figure).

morphology.note: No micrographs; eggs and specimens shown as cards with sizes.
